  Tagma defines a combinational decoder that maps a 16-bit coordinate to a direct memory address
  in one cycle. The coordinate's three-axis structure admits unbounded recursive embedding: each
  axis of a SynTagma can itself be a full CoordPath, producing identifier spaces that exceed
  physically meaningful quantities at the first recursion level. This paper formalises the

  space imposes no bound on topology depth; the practical limit is a question of protocol
  design, memory hierarchy engineering, and network bandwidth.

## Introduction

Every identifier system must eventually cross a physical boundary. A single-chip decoder of
approximately 300 gates maps a Coord to a direct memory address in one cycle. This is Tagma's
core contribution: identity that costs less than a single multiply. But the address space of a
single decoder is bounded by its syllable count. The Tagma composition formula $C(i,m,f)$
admits unbounded $k$ levels of recursion — a 19-syllable CoordPath at $k=1$ produces $S_1
\approx 7.30 \times 10^{231}$ distinct addresses — but a single memory controller, a single bus, or a single die cannot hold $10^{231}$
entries.

SynTagma is the layer that resolves this tension. It does not redefine the composition formula,
the CoordPath linearisation, or the sparse allocation scheme; those are properties of the core
Tagma specification [@tagma-wp]. SynTagma defines how the same arithmetic is mapped onto a
physical topology: when three axes of a SynTagma triplet reside on different nodes, how the
CoordPath is routed, what transport framing carries coordinates across a link, and what
consistency model governs concurrent access.

The relationship is structural. Tagma core defines the invariant: injectivity, closure under
recursion, zero collision probability. SynTagma defines the protocol: routing, framing,
resolution, and coordination. The invariant holds regardless of how many nodes participate. The
protocol is the engineering of that participation.

## Physical Topology Mapping

A SynTagma at recursion level $k$ is a Cartesian product of three CoordPaths at level $k-1$:

$$\mathbb{T}_k = \mathbb{T}_{k-1} \times \mathbb{T}_{k-1} \times \mathbb{T}_{k-1}$$

Each factor $\mathbb{T}_{k-1}$ is a set of valid CoordPaths at the previous level. The three
factors correspond to the three structural axes — initial, medial, final — that define a Tagma
coordinate at every level. Access follows the recursive linearisation formula:

$$\text{index}(a,b,c) = a \cdot S_{k-1}^2 + b \cdot S_{k-1} + c$$

where each of $a,b,c$ is itself an index into $\mathbb{T}_{k-1}$, computed recursively until
atomic Coords are reached.

**Physical binding.** The three axes of a SynTagma triplet need not reside on the same physical
device. Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a set of physical nodes. A topology mapping is a function:

$$\phi_k: \{i,m,f\} \rightarrow \mathcal{N}$$

that assigns each axis of a level-$k$ triplet to a physical node. Two axes mapped to the same
node are resolved locally; axes mapped to different nodes require transport. The assignment is
not fixed per formula — it is a deployment parameter determined by the physical arrangement of
decoder instances, memory controllers, and network links.

A CoordPath of length $3k \cdot N$ syllables can be interpreted as a traversal of $k$ topology
layers. At each layer, the three axis CoordPaths are dispatched to their assigned nodes for
recursive resolution. The total access cost is the sum of:

- local decode cost per syllable (one cycle per syllable)
- transport cost per axis boundary crossing (link latency)

For $k=1$ with a 19-syllable base and all three axes on one node, the cost is $3 \times 19 =
57$ array index operations. For the same base with axes spread across three nodes, the cost
adds two link traversals to the local decode.

## Transport and Routing

When a SynTagma triplet's axes are distributed, the resolving node must issue sub-requests to
the nodes holding each axis CoordPath. The transport layer carries these sub-requests and their
responses.

**Request format.** A SynTagma transport request carries:

| Field | Width | Description |
|-------|-------|-------------|
| CoordPath | $2N$ bytes | The axis CoordPath to resolve ($N$ syllables) |
| Axis tag | 2 bits | Which axis of the parent triplet (initial, medial, final) |
| Depth | $k$ | Remaining recursion depth |
| Transaction ID | 64 bits | Correlates responses |

The CoordPath is serialised as a sequence of 16-bit code points (U+AC00 base), maintaining the
structural validity property: every 16-bit value in the payload is independently verifiable as a
valid or invalid coordinate. Invalid values are rejected at the transport level before any
decoder access occurs.

**Self-routing property.** A CoordPath carries its own address. No separate routing table lookup
is required to determine which node holds a particular axis. The topology mapping function
$\phi_k$ is a deployment-time parameter distributed to all participating nodes. Given a
CoordPath and the current recursion depth, any node can determine whether each sub-axis is local
or remote by applying $\phi_k$ to the axis index derived from the CoordPath's linearisation.
Routing information is not embedded in the packets, because the coordinate structure is itself
the address.

This property distinguishes SynTagma from conventional content-addressable networks (CANs)
[@ratnasamy2001can] and distributed hash tables (DHTs) [@stoica2001chord], which require
topology-aware key assignment and iterative lookup hops. A SynTagma triplet's three axes are
named at composition time, before deployment; the topology mapping is a separate concern.

**Response coalescing.** The resolving node receives three axis responses and combines them via
the recursive linearisation formula. Because the arithmetic is closed form and independent of
the axis origins, coalescing is a single multiply-add per axis — no ordering or consensus is
required.

## Distributed Resolver

A node that receives a CoordPath for resolution executes the following procedure:

1. **Decompose.** Split the CoordPath into three axis CoordPaths at recursion level $k$.
2. **Map.** For each axis, apply $\phi_k$ to determine the target node.
3. **Dispatch.** Issue transport requests for axes mapped to remote nodes. Resolve local axes
   in-place via the Tagma decoder.
4. **Coalesce.** Wait for all remote responses, then compute: $\text{index} = a \cdot S_{k-1}^2
   - b \cdot S_{k-1} + c$.
5. **Recurse.** If $k > 1$, each axis CoordPath is itself resolved by recursively applying
   steps 1-4. If $k = 0$, return the atomic Coord index.

The resolver requires no global lock, no distributed consensus round, and no coordinator
election. Each resolution is a fixed-depth tree of independent local accesses and point-to-point
transport requests. The number of transport round-trips is bounded by $3^k$, one per axis per
recursion level.

**Caching.** Because the composition formula is injective and deterministic, two resolutions of
the same CoordPath on the same topology always produce the same index. Nodes may cache resolved
indices at any recursion depth. A cache hit at level $k$ eliminates all sub-requests below that
level. The cache key is the CoordPath fragment; the cache value is the index. No invalidation is
needed because the mapping is immutable — the composition formula does not change, and the
topology mapping $\phi_k$ is deployment-static.

## Distributed Identifier Generation

The entropy preservation analysis from the core specification applies directly to distributed
identifier generation in SynTagma. A summary of the relevant result:

A single true-random coord — one of 11,172 values, approximately $\log_2 11172 \approx 13.4$ bits
of entropy — placed in one axis of a SynTagma triplet is sufficient to make the full identifier
unpredictable, while the remaining axes can be filled with deterministic values such as device
identifier, sequence number, or timestamp. The resulting identifier inherits the unpredictability
of the random axis, while its uniqueness follows from the arithmetic injectivity of the
composition formula, not from the entropy of the input.

This property is practically important in distributed settings because it eliminates the need
for a central entropy source or a coordination protocol for identifier generation. Each node
generates identifiers independently using its own local entropy for one axis and its deterministic
node identity for the remaining axes. Two nodes with different deterministic values never
produce the same CoordPath, because the composition formula is injective over all axes.

The limitation is that each identifier consumes fresh entropy only from the random axis. A node
generating $m$ identifiers must consume $m \times \log_2 11172$ bits of entropy. For high-volume
generators, this constrains throughput to the rate of the local TRNG. A node may reduce entropy
consumption by reusing the same random coord as a seed for a local deterministic counter in
another axis — equivalently, structuring the CoordPath as:

$$(\text{random}, \text{node\_id}, \text{sequence\_number})$$

where only the first axis draws from the TRNG and the remaining axes are deterministic. The
injectivity of the formula guarantees collision freedom across all axes regardless of which
axis carries entropy.

## Consistency Model

A distributed CoordMap supports three operations: insert, lookup, and delete. Each operation
targets a CoordPath — a specific address in the coordinate space.

**Immutability of the coordinate space.** The coordinate space $\mathbb{T}_k$ is a mathematical
object. Its structure — the set of valid addresses — does not change when data is inserted or
removed. Only the occupancy of each address changes: whether a particular CoordPath maps to
stored data or to an empty slot. This property follows from the sparse allocation scheme of the
underlying CoordMap, which allocates child nodes only along written paths.

**Per-node linearisability.** Each physical node's local CoordMap is linearisable: reads and
writes to the same CoordPath on the same node appear to occur in some total order. This is the
same guarantee as a conventional hash table or key-value store on a single machine.

**Cross-node invariants.** A SynTagma triplet spanning multiple nodes has no cross-node
consistency requirement for reads, because the recursive linearisation formula is a pure
function of the three axis indices. Reading axis $a$ from node A and axis $b$ from node B
requires no coordination: the index computation $a \cdot S_{k-1}^2 + b \cdot S_{k-1} + c$ is
deterministic regardless of when each axis value is read.

Write operations that affect axes on different nodes require no distributed transaction,
because each axis CoordPath is an independent address subspace. Writing to axis $a$ affects
only node A's local CoordMap; writing to axis $b$ affects only node B's. A stale read across axes produces no anomaly, because no cross-axis invariant
constrains them.

**Absence of distributed consensus.** SynTagma does not require Paxos, Raft, or any
other distributed consensus protocol. The coordinate arithmetic is a pure function of its
inputs, which are independently stored and independently accessed per axis. Coordination is
required only when two nodes attempt to write to the same CoordPath on the same node, which
reduces to per-node concurrency control — a solved problem for a single-machine key-value
store.

## Boundaries

SynTagma does not define:

**A network protocol.** Transport framing, retransmission, flow control, and congestion
avoidance are outside SynTagma's scope. A SynTagma transport request can be carried by
HTTP/2, gRPC, QUIC, RDMA, or a dedicated raw Ethernet frame. The choice is a deployment
parameter.

**Topology discovery.** How nodes learn about each other and exchange $\phi_k$ mappings is
not part of the SynTagma specification. In static deployments, $\phi_k$ is a configuration
file. In dynamic deployments, it requires a separate discovery service.

**Authentication or encryption.** SynTagma transport requests carry CoordPaths, not secrets.
A node that receives a transport request must trust the requesting node's identity or verify
it through external mechanisms. Tagma's structural validity check verifies that each coord
in the path is a valid coordinate, but it does not authenticate the sender.

**Data replication.** A distributed CoordMap stores each CoordPath value on exactly one node
(the node that holds the axis where the value is written). Replication for fault tolerance is
outside SynTagma's scope and must be provided by the storage layer.

## Conclusion

SynTagma is the coordination layer that maps Tagma's recursive coordinate arithmetic onto
physical topologies. The mapping is defined by three components: the topology function
$\phi_k$ that assigns each axis of a SynTagma triplet to a physical node, the transport format
that carries CoordPath fragments between nodes, and the resolver procedure that assembles
distributed axis responses through the recursive linearisation formula.

The resulting system has two properties that distinguish it from conventional distributed
identifier systems. First, the identifier is self-routing: a CoordPath carries its own
address, and routing reduces to applying the topology function at each recursion level. Second,
the coordinate arithmetic is a pure function of independent axis values, so cross-node reads
and writes require no distributed consensus. The consistency model reduces to per-node
linearisability.

The formula admits unbounded $k$. Reaching $k=2$, $k=3$, or further is a question of
transport latency, topology engineering, and bandwidth — not of mathematical possibility. SynTagma defines the protocol structure within which those engineering decisions
are made.
